questions.q: Besides the questions a traditional application threat model already asks, what three dimensions does an AI-specific threat model add?
options: Server rack location, power consumption, and cooling capacity
Programming language used, number of developers, and code repository size
Monitor resolution, keyboard layout, and operating system version
Data sensitivity (training/retrieved/memorized data), autonomy level, and user trust boundary
questions.explain: An AI-specific threat model layers on what the model was trained/retrieves/could memorize, how much autonomous action it can take, and who is allowed to interact with it at what trust level.

questions.q: In STRIDE adapted for AI components, what does the Tampering category typically correspond to?
options: Prompt injection altering the model's behavior at inference time, or data poisoning altering it at training time
Only physical tampering with server hardware in a data center
A user changing their own display name in a support ticket
A model's GPU running at a higher-than-expected clock speed
questions.explain: Tampering, in an AI context, maps onto prompt injection (altering behavior at inference time) and data poisoning (altering behavior through the training pipeline).

questions.q: Why does autonomy level matter when building a threat model for an AI system?
options: Because only chatbots with no tool access can ever be attacked
Because autonomy level only affects how fast the model generates text, not security risk
It doesn't — every AI system has the same blast radius regardless of what actions it can take
Because the blast radius of a successful attack scales directly with how much real-world action the system can take on its own
questions.explain: A read-only chatbot and an agent that can call tools or execute actions have very different consequences if compromised — autonomy directly scales the impact of a successful attack.

questions.q: In the worked refund-ticket chatbot example, why was Elevation of Privilege flagged as a top-priority STRIDE category?
options: Because the system is read-only and cannot take any real action
Because the chatbot can call a create-refund-ticket API — it is not read-only, so an attacker manipulating that tool call has a real, costly consequence
Because the chatbot could not retrieve any data from the knowledge base at all
Because refund tickets are always reviewed manually before any action is taken, eliminating risk
questions.explain: The chatbot's ability to call a real API (create a refund ticket) means tampering that manipulates that tool call escalates into an elevation-of-privilege risk with a genuine financial consequence.

questions.q: What is the practical output of building an AI-specific threat model, as described in this lesson?
options: It is purely a documentation exercise with no effect on how testing is scoped
It eliminates the need for any red-team testing on the system
It tells a red-team engagement where to concentrate its test cases, instead of testing every component equally
It replaces the need to classify any data the system touches
questions.explain: The threat model surfaces concrete, prioritized risks for a specific system, which is exactly what feeds the scope of the red-team engagement covered in the previous lesson.
